heroBody: OLED remains the picture-quality reference for TV in 2026: per-pixel light control, infinite contrast, perfect black levels and wide viewing angles. The US OLED market has consolidated to three panel makers — LG Display, Samsung Display and Sony-branded panels built on those — and a half-dozen TV brands that use them. Pricing runs from mid-three-figures on a 55-inch entry model to four-figure sums on a 65-inch or 77-inch flagship, with the deepest discounts at the 65-inch size where the panel volume is highest. This page pulls live listings from BuyWhere's catalog every few minutes so the price on each card is what US retailers are actually charging right now, not a static snapshot from earlier in the year.

highlightSectionTitle: What changed with OLED TVs in 2026

highlights.title: Brightness is no longer the OLED compromise
highlights.body: Early OLED TVs were dimmer than the best LED-LCD TVs and that gap was visible in bright rooms. The latest generations of LG, Samsung and Sony OLED panels reach sustained full-screen brightness levels that match or beat mid-range LED-LCD sets, while keeping the per-pixel contrast that defines OLED. For most living rooms the brightness gap is no longer a reason to avoid OLED.

highlights.title: WOLED versus QD-OLED
highlights.body: LG Display's WOLED panels use a white OLED stack with colour filters; Samsung Display's QD-OLED panels use blue OLED with quantum-dot colour conversion. Both approaches deliver excellent picture quality and the gap between them has narrowed year over year. Pick on price, panel size and brand support rather than getting hung up on the panel technology underneath.

highlights.title: Bigger sizes are no longer rare
highlights.body: Three years ago, OLED TVs above 77 inches were a niche premium product. In 2026, 83-inch and 97-inch OLED panels are regularly available at major US retailers, with manufacturer-refurbished and open-box deals bringing the price within reach of buyers who would previously have bought a mid-range LED-LCD.

adviceSectionTitle: How to pick an OLED TV without overspending
advicePoints: Buy the 65-inch size if you sit 2-3 metres from the screen. The 65-inch OLED is where panel volume is highest and discounts are deepest; the per-inch value is almost always the best at this size.

Decide on HDMI count and HDMI 2.1. Modern OLED TVs have at least one HDMI 2.1 port for 4K at 120Hz gaming; if you own a current-generation console and a soundbar, you may need two HDMI 2.1 ports, which not every model has.

Skip the manufacturer extended warranty on premium OLEDs if you buy from a US retailer with a strong return policy. Best Buy, B&H and Amazon all offer 30-day returns on TVs; if the panel has a defect you will see it in the first month.

Consider the sound. OLED panels are thin and the built-in speakers are usually mediocre; budget for a soundbar or a proper home-theatre setup. Some OLED TVs offer an HDMI eARC port and Dolby Atmos passthrough that high-end sound systems rely on.

Check burn-in coverage. Modern OLED panels include pixel-refresh cycles and screen-shift features that prevent burn-in for normal TV watching; the risk is mostly for users who display static news tickers or game HUDs at full brightness for many hours a day.
faqSectionTitle: OLED TVs in the US — common questions

faqs.question: Is OLED worth it over a good LED-LCD TV in the US?
faqs.answer: For picture quality in a dim or moderately lit room, yes. OLED's per-pixel contrast and viewing angles deliver a clearly better image than even the best LED-LCD at the same price. For a very bright room with lots of direct sunlight, a high-end LED-LCD with strong anti-reflective coating and high sustained brightness can be the smarter choice.

faqs.question: Which OLED TV size is the best value in the US?
faqs.answer: The 65-inch size is where panel volume is highest, retailer competition is strongest and per-inch value peaks. If your seating distance allows for 65 inches, that is the size to standardise on for the best balance of price and screen area.

faqs.question: Do OLED TVs burn in?
faqs.answer: Under normal TV viewing (movies, streaming, gaming without a static HUD at full brightness for many hours) modern OLED panels do not develop visible burn-in within the panel's useful life. Built-in pixel-refresh cycles and screen-shift features mitigate the risk for typical household use.

faqs.question: When is the cheapest time to buy an OLED TV in the US?
faqs.answer: Major sale events (Black Friday, Cyber Monday, Memorial Day, the Super Bowl window) bring the deepest discounts. Outside those windows the live prices on this page show the current floor.

categoryIntro.heading: Why OLED TV prices in the US swing so widely
categoryIntro.body: Three forces drive the spread between the cheapest and most expensive OLED TV listings on any given day in the US. First, panel size: the per-inch cost of an OLED panel drops sharply as you move from 55-inch to 65-inch and again to 77-inch, but the absolute price climbs. Second, retailer competition: Best Buy runs aggressive TV promotions around major sporting events, Amazon matches within hours, and B&H tends to hold the lowest price on open-box and manufacturer-refurbished stock. Third, model year: last year's flagship OLED drops meaningfully in price once the new line launches and remains an excellent TV for several more years. The live cards on this page read current listings rather than a stale 'best price' table so you can compare what is actually available right now.
